question: A DevOps team packages an application with only its libraries and dependencies so that it shares the host operating system kernel and starts in seconds. Which technology are they using?
explanation: containerization. Sharing the host kernel and bundling only the app plus its dependencies is the lightweight container model. The tell: containerization = shares host kernel, packages app plus deps; virtualization = full guest OS per VM on a hypervisor; serverless = provider runs your functions with no server to manage; microservices = one app split into small independent services.

question: A cloud model where the provider fully manages the underlying servers and runs your code as event-triggered functions billed per execution is called what?
explanation: serverless. No server to provision or manage plus per-execution billing of functions is the serverless model. The tell: serverless = provider runs functions, no server to manage; virtualization = full guest OS per VM; containerization = shares host kernel with bundled deps; microservices = app split into small independent services.

question: An operations team provisions and configures its entire cloud environment from declarative template files kept in version control, so rebuilds are fully automated and repeatable. What is this practice?
explanation: infrastructure as code (IaC). Provisioning infrastructure from declarative, version-controlled templates is IaC. The tell: infrastructure as code = provision infrastructure from code/templates; virtualization = full guest OS per VM; containerization = shares host kernel with bundled deps; microservices = app split into small independent services.

question: A defense contractor keeps a classified analysis workstation with no network cabling, no wireless, and data moved only by inspected removable media. Which isolation model is this?
explanation: air-gapped. A total physical disconnection from any network is an air gap. The tell: air-gapped = physically no network connection; logical segmentation = VLAN/subnet separation on shared hardware; SDN = software-controlled network via control/data plane split; on-premises = hosted in your own facility.

question: Separating departments into different VLANs and subnets that ride the same physical switches, with no physical isolation, is best described as what?
explanation: logical segmentation. Separating traffic by VLAN or subnet on shared hardware is logical, not physical, isolation. The tell: logical segmentation = VLAN/subnet separation on shared hardware; air-gapped = physically no network connection; SDN = software-controlled network via control/data plane split; decentralized = distributed control across many points.

question: A network team manages forwarding behavior centrally through a software controller that programs the switches, cleanly separating the control plane from the data plane. What is this?
explanation: SDN. Separating the control plane from the data plane and programming forwarding via a software controller defines software-defined networking. The tell: SDN = control/data plane split via software controller; air-gapped = no network connection at all; logical segmentation = VLAN/subnet separation; centralized = a single point of control generally.

question: A water utility uses a supervisory system to monitor and control pumping stations spread across hundreds of miles, collecting telemetry and issuing commands from a central control room. Which term fits best?
explanation: SCADA. Wide-area supervisory monitoring and control of remote industrial sites is SCADA. The tell: SCADA = wide-area supervisory layer that monitors/controls ICS; ICS = the industrial control systems running the physical process; IoT = internet-connected consumer/smart devices; RTOS = OS with guaranteed real-time timing.

question: An operating system that guarantees deterministic response within strict time limits, used in airbag controllers and medical infusion pumps, is called what?
explanation: RTOS. Guaranteed timing for real-time tasks is the defining trait of a real-time operating system. The tell: RTOS = OS with guaranteed real-time timing; embedded system = special-purpose computer inside a larger device; IoT = internet-connected smart devices; ICS = industrial control systems running physical processes.

question: The architectural property of absorbing component failures while continuing to serve users and recovering automatically is best described as what?
explanation: resilience. Continuing to serve and self-recover through failure is resilience, not simply being up right now. The tell: resilience = recover and keep serving under failure; availability = uptime at this moment; scalability = grow to handle more load; responsiveness = latency of the response.

question: Unable to fully eliminate a threat, an organization buys cyber insurance to shift the financial impact of a potential breach to a third party. Which architecture consideration does this reflect?
explanation: risk transference. Shifting the financial impact to a third party such as an insurer is risk transference. The tell: risk transference = shift risk to a third party (insurance/vendor); resilience = recover and keep serving under failure; scalability = grow to handle more load; cost = the expense of the design itself.

question: A network firewall loses connectivity to its management system and, by configuration, continues to pass all traffic so the business stays online. Which behavior is this?
explanation: fail-open. Permitting traffic on failure to favor availability is fail-open. The tell: fail-open = permits traffic on failure (favors availability); fail-closed = blocks traffic on failure (favors security), the network pair with fail-open; fail-secure = a physical lock that stays locked on power loss to protect assets; fail-safe = a physical lock that unlocks on power loss to protect people.

question: When a data center loses power, the electronic maglocks on its doors release so occupants can evacuate. Because the design prioritizes protecting human life over securing the room, which failure mode term best describes it?
explanation: fail-safe. Unlocking on power loss to protect human life is fail-safe. The tell: fail-safe = physical lock unlocks on power loss to protect people (life safety); fail-secure = physical lock stays locked on power loss to protect assets; fail-open = network control that permits traffic on failure; fail-closed = network control that blocks traffic on failure.

question: A network access control gateway is configured so that if it cannot reach its policy server, it denies all traffic rather than risk letting anything through. Which behavior is this?
explanation: fail-closed. Blocking traffic on failure to favor security is fail-closed, the network pair of fail-open. The tell: fail-closed = blocks traffic on failure (favors security); fail-open = permits traffic on failure (favors availability); fail-safe = physical lock unlocks on power loss for people; fail-secure = physical lock stays locked on power loss for assets.

question: A monitoring sensor is cabled to a switch SPAN port, where it receives a mirrored copy of network traffic rather than sitting in the traffic path. Which connection method is this?
explanation: tap/monitor. Receiving a mirrored copy via a SPAN port or tap, unable to affect the live flow, is a tap/monitor deployment. The tell: tap/monitor = receives a mirrored copy via SPAN/tap, cannot affect traffic; inline = traffic actually flows through the device; active = device role that can block; passive = device role that only observes.

question: A prevention appliance is installed directly in the traffic path so every packet must pass through it, allowing it to drop malicious packets in real time. Which deployment is this?
explanation: inline. Sitting in the path so all traffic flows through it is an inline deployment. The tell: inline = traffic flows through the device (can drop); tap/monitor = receives only a mirrored copy; active = the role of a device that can block; passive = observes only, cannot block.

question: Which term describes a device's role when it can only observe traffic and has no ability to block or modify it?
explanation: passive. A device that only observes and cannot block is passive by role. The tell: passive = observes only, cannot block (role); active = in-path role that can block; inline = deployment where traffic flows through; tap/monitor = deployment receiving a mirrored copy.

question: Unlike a proxy server, which brokers and filters client requests to services, which system is a hardened gateway host that administrators connect through to reach internal machines?
explanation: jump server. A hardened admin pivot host you connect through to manage internal systems is a jump server. The tell: jump server = hardened admin pivot host you connect through; proxy server = intermediary that forwards/filters client requests; reverse proxy = sits in front of servers handling inbound client requests; forward proxy = sits in front of internal clients making outbound requests.

question: An appliance placed in front of an organization's web servers accepts all inbound client requests, filters them, caches frequently requested content, and shields the servers' internal addresses. Which system is this?
explanation: reverse proxy. Brokering inbound client traffic in front of servers, with filtering, caching, and server shielding, is a reverse proxy. The tell: reverse proxy = broker in front of servers for inbound client traffic; forward proxy = broker in front of internal clients for outbound requests; load balancer = distributes requests across multiple servers for throughput, not a request filter; jump server = hardened admin gateway pivot host.

question: Internal users' outbound web requests all route through a device that filters and caches them on the clients' behalf before they reach the internet. Which system is this?
explanation: forward proxy. Brokering internal clients' outbound requests with filtering and caching is a forward proxy. The tell: forward proxy = broker for internal clients' outbound requests; reverse proxy = broker in front of servers for inbound traffic; load balancer = distributes inbound requests across multiple servers for throughput; jump server = hardened admin gateway pivot host.

question: An IDS and this control share the same detection engine, but this one is placed inline and actively drops malicious packets before they reach hosts. Which control is it?
explanation: IPS. Same detection as an IDS but inline with the power to block makes it an IPS. The tell: IPS = inline network control that detects and blocks; IDS = detects and alerts only, passive and out of band; HIDS = host-based detection/alert on one system; HIPS = host-based prevention that blocks locally on one host.

question: A sensor on a SPAN port watches network traffic and raises alerts when it sees suspicious patterns, but it is out of band and cannot stop anything. Which control is this?
explanation: IDS. Out-of-band detection and alerting with no ability to block is an IDS. The tell: IDS = passive network detection and alerting, out of band; IPS = inline network detection that also blocks; HIDS = host-based detection/alert only; HIPS = host-based prevention that blocks on one host.

question: A HIPS can block threats locally on a host. Which control also runs on a single host but only monitors and alerts, taking no blocking action?
explanation: HIDS. A host agent that only detects and alerts, without blocking, is a HIDS. The tell: HIDS = host-based detection/alert only on one system; HIPS = host-based control that also blocks locally; IDS = network-wide detection/alert only; IPS = inline network detection that blocks.

question: A security team deploys a device specifically to inspect HTTP requests to a public web application and block SQL injection and cross-site scripting attempts. Which device is this?
explanation: WAF. Protecting a web application from injection and cross-site scripting at the application layer is a web application firewall. The tell: WAF = protects web apps from injection/XSS at Layer 7; NGFW = app-aware firewall with deep inspection and identity; UTM = all-in-one appliance bundling many security functions; Layer 4 firewall = filters only by port and IP.

question: A single all-in-one appliance that bundles firewalling, antivirus, intrusion prevention, and content filtering into one box is known as what?
explanation: UTM. Bundling many security functions into one appliance is unified threat management. The tell: UTM = one appliance bundling many security functions; WAF = protects web apps from injection/XSS; NGFW = app-aware firewall with deep packet inspection and identity; Layer 7 firewall = filters by application-layer content.

question: A Layer 4 firewall filters only by port and IP address. Which firewall type extends this with application awareness, deep packet inspection, and user identity integration?
explanation: NGFW. Adding application awareness, deep inspection, and identity to traditional filtering defines a next-generation firewall. The tell: NGFW = adds app awareness, deep inspection, and identity; Layer 4 firewall = filters only by port and IP; WAF = protects web apps from injection/XSS; UTM = all-in-one bundle of security functions.

question: The standard that keeps a switch port or wireless association blocked until the connecting device successfully authenticates is called what?
explanation: 802.1X. Port-based access control that holds the port closed until authentication succeeds is 802.1X. The tell: 802.1X = the port gate that stays closed until authentication succeeds; EAP = the authentication framework 802.1X carries; PEAP = an EAP method tunneling credentials in server-side TLS; EAP-TLS = an EAP method requiring mutual client and server certificates.

question: 802.1X does not define the actual authentication exchange itself; instead it transports a flexible framework within which methods like PEAP and EAP-TLS operate. What is that framework?
explanation: EAP. The extensible authentication framework carried by 802.1X, under which specific methods run, is EAP. The tell: EAP = the authentication framework carried by 802.1X; 802.1X = the port gate that invokes it; PEAP = a specific EAP method tunneling in server-side TLS; EAP-TLS = a specific EAP method using mutual certificates.

question: Remote employees connect to internal applications through a browser over TCP port 443, with no full VPN client installed on their machines. Which tunneling technology is this?
explanation: TLS VPN. A transport-layer tunnel over port 443 that is clientless-friendly is a TLS VPN. The tell: TLS VPN = transport/application-layer tunnel over port 443, clientless-friendly; IPSec = network-layer tunnel using AH/ESP, common for site-to-site; SD-WAN = software-defined WAN link optimization between sites; SASE = SD-WAN converged with cloud-delivered security.

question: Two data centers are connected by a permanent encrypted tunnel operating at the network layer using ESP for confidentiality and integrity. Which technology is this?
explanation: IPSec. A network-layer tunnel using ESP for site-to-site connectivity is IPSec. The tell: IPSec = network-layer tunnel (AH/ESP), site-to-site; TLS VPN = transport-layer tunnel over port 443; SD-WAN = software-defined WAN optimization between sites; SASE = SD-WAN plus cloud-delivered security as one service.

question: A software-defined overlay that dynamically steers branch traffic across multiple transport links such as MPLS, broadband, and LTE to optimize performance and cost is called what?
explanation: SD-WAN. Software-defined steering of WAN traffic across multiple links to optimize sites is SD-WAN. The tell: SD-WAN = software-defined WAN that optimizes links between sites; SASE = SD-WAN combined with cloud-delivered security (ZTNA, SWG, CASB); IPSec = network-layer encrypted tunnel; TLS VPN = transport-layer tunnel over port 443.

question: A company adopts a single cloud-delivered service that combines SD-WAN connectivity with security functions like zero-trust network access, secure web gateway, and CASB. Which model is this?
explanation: SASE. Converging SD-WAN with cloud-delivered security into one service is SASE. The tell: SASE = SD-WAN converged with cloud-delivered security (ZTNA/SWG/CASB) as one service; SD-WAN = the connectivity/link-optimization layer alone; IPSec = network-layer encrypted tunnel; TLS VPN = transport-layer clientless-friendly tunnel.
